passage:
Monday: For the third time, Vijay told the team that Ishita had "invented" a deadline he had set. Ishita went pink and apologised, then sat in the washroom wondering if her memory was going.
Thursday: That evening she opened a private notebook at home and wrote: date, what was said, who was there. She added the old ones too: 3 March, deadline given in standup, Neel present. She called her friend Soumya and read it out. "You're not making this up," Soumya said. "You have dates."
Three weeks later, Tuesday: Vijay tried again. "I never asked for the draft by today." Ishita kept her voice level. "You asked in Friday's standup, and your email that afternoon says so." She forwarded it. Vijay went quiet. That evening she booked a session with the company counsellor, to plan what to do if it kept happening.

qa.q: Who was present when the deadline was given on 3 March?
qa.a: Neel was present at the standup.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel after the first incident?
qa.a: Ishita felt embarrassed and shaken, going pink and wondering in the washroom whether her memory was going.

qa.q: Which of Ishita's steps protected her own perception?
qa.a: Writing dates and witnesses privately, checking the notes with Soumya, and keeping the email gave her anchors outside Vijay's version.

qa.q: What would change if Ishita had kept everything to herself?
qa.a: Without notes, the email or a friend's check, Ishita might have kept apologising and doubting her memory, and Vijay's account would have gone unchallenged.

grounding: Shows a person keeping a private record of dates and events, checking it with a trusted friend and a counsellor, so reality rests on anchors other than the doubter.

passage:
Coach's note, university badminton squad, Friday.
Vidya and Jatin (mixed doubles) disagreed on Monday about who covers the back court. Since then Vidya has not spoken to Jatin at all: no eye contact, turning away at drinks breaks, answering his questions only through me. Jatin has apologised twice, each time more anxiously; on Wednesday he offered to switch to the front court "if that fixes it". Vidya looked satisfied, but stayed silent.
After practice today I asked Vidya to stay back and asked what the silence was doing for her. She took a long time, then said, "When I stop talking, he comes round. When I argue, I lose." She seemed surprised to hear herself say it.
We agreed she will tell Jatin what she actually wants on court, in words, by Monday. I will sit in if both want. I will check in with Jatin separately too.

qa.q: What did Jatin offer on Wednesday?
qa.a: He offered to switch to the front court if that fixes it.

qa.q: What did Vidya's answer reveal about her silence?
qa.a: Vidya seemed to feel powerless in arguments and in control when silent; she looked surprised, even uneasy, hearing herself say it.

qa.q: How did the coach respond, and why does it help?
qa.a: The coach asked Vidya privately what the silence was doing, then agreed a plan for her to state her wishes in words by Monday, with an offer to sit in and a separate check on Jatin.

qa.q: What is it like for Jatin under the silence?
qa.a: Jatin seems anxious and keeps apologising, even offering to change position, just to make the silence end.

grounding: Shows a young adult going silent after a disagreement so the other pleads and gives in, using silence as power when arguing felt risky.

subtype: Asking for a pause versus stonewalling [Response]
passage:
Sunday, 10:50 pm
Big fight with Tenzin tonight about moving to Bengaluru for her job. My voice was getting loud, my jaw was tight, and I could feel the old urge: walk out, go silent for two days, let her come to me. That's what I did last winter, and she told me later it felt like being punished with no end.
So I said it the way the counsellor practised with me: "I'm too angry to talk well. I need one hour. I'll be back at ten." Tenzin looked scared, then nodded.
I walked around the lake, called nobody, just breathed. At ten I knocked on the bedroom door. We sat on the floor and talked till now. Nothing's decided. But she said, "You came back when you said you would," and her face softened.
Setting the hour felt awkward. The two-day silence used to feel powerful. Only one of them felt kind.
Uday

qa.q: What time did Uday promise to be back?
qa.a: Uday said, “I'll be back at ten.”

qa.q: What was Uday feeling just before asking for the hour?
qa.a: Uday felt angry, with a loud voice and tight jaw, and tempted to go silent for two days as a punishment.

qa.q: Why does saying one hour and back at ten work better than walking out?
qa.a: It is a break with a clear promise to return, so Tenzin is not left in an endless silence that demands surrender.

qa.q: How did Tenzin experience the pause compared with last winter?
qa.a: Last winter the silence felt like being punished with no end; this time Tenzin looked scared at first but softened when Uday came back as promised.

grounding: Shows a person asking for an hour to calm down with a promise to return, unlike the punishing silence with no end used before.

passage:
"Hrithik, can I tell you something? But don't say I said it." Lalremsiami leaned on the lab counter.
"Okay..."
"Mawii told me she only sits with you because you help with maths."
Hrithik's pencil stopped. "She said that?"
"Kind of. Basically. I just think you should know who your real friends are."
"Why didn't you tell her it was mean?"
"I'm telling you, aren't I?"
Hrithik frowned. "You and Mawii fought yesterday, right? About the fest group?"
Lalremsiami felt her face heat. "That's not the point."
"Feels like it's the point. If you're angry with her, talk to her. Don't make me pick."
He went back to his diagram. Lalremsiami stared at her shoes. She had wanted him on her side so Mawii would feel alone the way she had yesterday. Hearing it out loud, it sounded small.
"Fine," she muttered. "I'll talk to her at lunch."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami claim Mawii said?
qa.a: That Mawii only sits with Hrithik because he helps with maths.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami go to Hrithik instead of Mawii?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt hurt and angry after yesterday's fight and wanted Mawii to feel alone too, so pulling Hrithik onto her side felt safer than talking directly.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do well?
qa.a: He noticed the fight behind the message, refused to pick a side, and pushed Lalremsiami to talk to Mawii herself.

qa.q: How might Mawii feel if Hrithik had believed the message?
qa.a: Mawii could have lost a friend without knowing why, feeling confused and shut out over words she may never have said.

grounding: Shows a teenager carrying a hurtful message to a third person to gain an ally after a fight, because direct talk felt risky.

subtype: Being compared or used as a go-between [Receiver]
passage: In the hostel visitors' room, Chandrika sat with her phone on speaker while her roommate Charu pretended to read. "Tell your father," her mother said, "that if he can afford a new car, he can afford your fees on time. Tell him exactly that." Chandrika's stomach dropped. Last week her father had asked her to "mention" to her mother that she'd always been bad with money. Every Sunday call now came with a message to carry. "Amma, can you tell him yourself?" "Why should I talk to that man? You're his daughter." After the call, Chandrika pressed her palms into her eyes. "If I pass it on, Papa gets angry at me. If I don't, Amma says I've taken his side." Charu put the book down. "You're not their post office. The student counsellor sees people for exactly this. Want me to come with you tomorrow?" Chandrika nodded, slowly.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's mother want her to tell her father?
qa.a: That if he can afford a new car, he can afford her fees on time.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling after the call?
qa.a: Chandrika felt anxious and torn between her parents: passing it on makes Papa angry, and refusing makes Amma say she's taken his side.

qa.q: What could help Chandrika step out of the go-between role?
qa.a: She could tell each parent kindly that she won't carry messages, and take up Charu's offer to see the student counsellor for support.

qa.q: How does Charu see the situation?
qa.a: Charu sees Chandrika being used as a post office between her parents and offers practical support by going to the counsellor together.

grounding: Shows a young adult used by parents to carry hurtful messages to each other, left anxious and torn in loyalty.

passage: At the weekly haat in their village near Jorhat, Rajni caught Bhupen by the vegetable stalls. "You're close to Hemanta-da," she said, lowering her voice. "Tell him the self-help group knows he kept the best stall spot for his wife. Everyone's saying it. He'll listen to you." Bhupen set down his bag of brinjals. Hemanta-da and Rajni had been at odds since the Bihu committee. Carrying this, he could see, would make him a messenger in a quarrel he had never joined. "Baideo, if you think it's unfair, say it to him yourself," he said gently. "I can sit with you both after the group meeting on Sunday if that helps. But I won't carry a message either way, from you or from him." Rajni's mouth tightened. "So you're on his side." "I'm on nobody's side. That's the point." On Sunday, she came to the meeting early.

qa.q: What did Rajni want Bhupen to tell Hemanta-da?
qa.a: That the self-help group knows he kept the best stall spot for his wife.

qa.q: What was Bhupen thinking as he set down the brinjals?
qa.a: Bhupen felt wary and uneasy, seeing that carrying the message would make him a messenger in a quarrel he had never joined.

qa.q: Why was offering to sit with them both a wise move?
qa.a: It sent the complaint back to its source while still offering support, and refusing messages from either side kept Bhupen out of the fight.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt when Bhupen refused?
qa.a: Rajni felt rebuffed and suspicious at first, accusing him of taking Hemanta-da's side, yet coming early on Sunday suggests she accepted talking directly.

grounding: Shows a person asked to carry a grievance who suggests the two talk directly and declines to take sides.

passage: In the school library during free period, Akash finally said it. "Shalini, the history model is due tomorrow and your part isn't done. We've asked three times." Shalini's eyes filled at once. "Wow. You know I've had the worst week. Nobody ever asks how I am. I always get blamed for everything in every group." The others shifted. Tanu passed her a tissue; someone murmured, "Sorry, Shalu." Akash looked at the table, suddenly the bad guy. Later, walking to the bus alone, Shalini replayed it. She had forgotten the model; that was the truth. But saying "I forgot" had felt like the floor opening under her, like proof she was useless. The tears had come before she chose them. Now everyone was comforting her, and the model still wasn't made. She took out her phone, then put it back, not yet able to type the word sorry.

qa.q: How many times had the group asked about Shalini's part?
qa.a: They had asked three times.

qa.q: Why did saying she forgot feel so hard for Shalini?
qa.a: Shalini feared it was proof of being useless; that shame about being at fault made the tears come before she chose them.

qa.q: What could Shalini do now to repair things?
qa.a: She could message the group, admit she forgot, say sorry plainly and offer to finish her part tonight, instead of turning the complaint into sympathy.

qa.q: How did Akash seem to feel after the others comforted Shalini?
qa.a: Akash seemed embarrassed and uncomfortable, looking at the table, as if a fair reminder had made him the bad guy.

grounding: Shows a teenager turning a fair complaint into sympathy for herself because being at fault feels unbearable.

passage:
Dear Vinita didi,
Remember in June when Rhea and I didn't talk for a whole month because I kept arguing that the scooty dent wasn't really my fault? You said next time, try just saying sorry and see what happens. I tried it this week.
I posted a group photo from the picnic where Kavin had his eyes half shut and food on his shirt. He messaged me, really upset. My first reply was already typed: "It's just a photo, chill." I deleted it. I wrote: "You're right, I should have asked. Sorry. I've taken it down."
He called me something rude in his first message, and I did tell him that part wasn't okay. But I didn't pretend the photo was his fault.
By evening he sent a funny sticker and we were normal again. One day instead of one month!
Love,
Ira

qa.q: What reply had Ira typed before deleting it?
qa.a: “It's just a photo, chill.”

qa.q: How did Ira feel about how quickly things recovered with Kavin?
qa.a: Ira felt relieved and pleased, even surprised, that a plain sorry fixed things in one day instead of one month.

qa.q: How did Ira balance owning the mistake with not taking all the blame?
qa.a: Ira apologised plainly and took the photo down, but also told Kavin his rude word wasn't okay, taking responsibility without accepting blame that wasn't Ira's.

qa.q: How might Kavin have felt if he had received the first reply?
qa.a: Kavin would likely have felt dismissed and more hurt, and the quarrel might have dragged on like the month with Rhea.

grounding: Shows a teenager owning a mistake with a plain sorry and finding the friendship recovers faster than it did through defensiveness.
